title: Ralph Loops: Build Dumb AI Loops That Ship — Chris Parsons, Cherrypick
talk_summary: Chris Parsons demonstrates 'Ralph loops': running a coding agent in a dumb loop over a ticket backlog, letting it pick the next most important ticket and iterate, rather than hand-orchestrating dependencies or building complex workflow graphs. He argues the loop's quality comes entirely from the prompt/skill (feedback criteria, stop conditions, recovery states) and that sub-agents with fresh context beat self-review.

takeaways.technique: Let the agent pick the next ticket instead of pre-computing dependencies
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of building a dependency graph across tickets and dispatching parallel agents (which caused duplicate work and contention), the loop prompt simply says 'pick the next most important ticket' and the model resolves dependencies on the fly from current repo state.
takeaways.evidence_quote: just pick the next most important ticket ... The AI is quite capable of looking at all of them, figuring out the dependencies on the fly

takeaways.technique: Adversarial validation in a fresh-context sub-agent
takeaways.what_they_do: Validation done in the same session as implementation just rubber-stamps itself; running the check as a sub-agent that starts with only a small slice of context surfaces real defects. Claude's bundled 'simplify' skill spawns three sub-agents to critique recent changes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: as soon as I changed mine to use sub agents here now for the validation step, it started finding things ... it just pats itself on the back

takeaways.technique: Codify the loop as a versioned skill with explicit stop/recovery states
takeaways.what_they_do: The real Ralph skill encodes role, ticket format, status values, git-state checks, and recovery rules (dirty tree + passing tests = probably done; failing tests = mid-flight, discard), plus explicit stop conditions: stop and report when context runs low or an irreversible action is next.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If the tests are failing ... it's probably just mid-flight and broken, so you should probably just throw it away

takeaways.technique: Make 'done' machine-checkable so the loop can self-terminate
takeaways.what_they_do: Loops work best on work with an objective pass/fail signal (CLI tool, tests, screenshots). He explicitly designs feedback mechanisms so the agent, not the human, can tell whether output is good; when he can remove himself from that loop it 'massively improves the whole process'.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I'm always looking to figure out how if an AI could tell whether something was good or not rather than me

takeaways.technique: Fresh context per unit of work; treat sessions as ephemeral
takeaways.what_they_do: Prefers a new session per ticket so nothing useful lives only in session history; forces knowledge to be codified into repo files any future session or human can find. Notes same-session loops are fine now that long-context retrieval is strong, but fresh context yields a richer knowledge repository.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if it has to pick up again from a fresh context, it means that all of the information that was in that session has actually been codified

takeaways.technique: Don't parallelize until the loop is the bottleneck
takeaways.what_they_do: His parallel multi-agent attempt failed with contention (two agents implementing the same shared ticket); he now runs one sequential loop and treats human review capacity, not agent count, as the constraint. Also applies theory of constraints: fix the actual bottleneck (e.g. release/review process) before adding agents.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the bottleneck is usually not the number of agents. It's usually you just keeping up with the AI
